props.title: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring
props.initialSlug: Buddhist monk's life journey through the seasons

sections.content: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring (2003) stands as Korean director Kim Ki-duk's masterpiece of Buddhist philosophy translated to cinema. The film's structure mirrors the seasons of life through a young monk's journey, filmed entirely on a floating monastery in a pristine lake. Like Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev (1966), it uses spiritual contemplation to explore human nature, but with a minimalist approach that recalls Ozu's Tokyo Story (1953). Each season represents a stage of life, with actions rippling across time in ways that evoke Three Times (2005) by Hou Hsiao-hsien.

movies.title: I Am a Monk
movies.slug: Contemporary look at a young Japanese man who inherits his family temple and struggles with modern monastery life

sections.content: The film's visual poetry draws from a rich tradition of East Asian cinema focused on spiritual journeys. The Burmese Harp (1956) similarly used Buddhism as a lens for examining war's impact on the soul, while Zen (2009) portrayed the life of Dogen with comparable attention to ritual and nature. Ki-duk's genius lies in stripping away dialogue to let images carry meaning - floating doors, stone burdens, and changing seasons become powerful metaphors without a word spoken. SUBHEAD: Contemplative Cinema and Sacred Spaces

This film belongs to a broader tradition of contemplative cinema that includes Into Great Silence (2005), which documented Carthusian monks through the seasons, and Departures (2008), exploring Japanese funeral rites. The floating monastery setting creates a liminal space between heaven and earth, much like the mountain temple in Seven Years in Tibet (1997). But unlike these films, Ki-duk uses his sacred space to tell a universal coming-of-age story, one where spiritual growth comes through confronting human desires and failings.
